\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Execution Traces for Code LLMs}

Recent work has scaled trace-augmented training: TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} pre-trained on 2.6M execution-annotated samples, while \citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained models to predict execution outputs from traces.
\citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility to be task- and format-dependent but did not decompose individual trace components; relative to their work, we contribute a two-tier signal hierarchy, a phase transition in trace-length budgets, calibration analysis, and cross-architecture validation.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} leveraged trace chain-of-thought for execution reasoning, and \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, aligning with our density finding.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, extended to 19 languages by CRUXEval-X \citep{xu2025cruxevalx}, established execution reasoning benchmarks, though neither decomposes which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.
\citet{shi2023distracted} showed LLMs are easily distracted by irrelevant context, providing a complementary explanation for why verbose traces impair SFT learning.
In the prompt compression literature, LLMLingua \citep{jiang2023llmlingua} and Selective Context \citep{li2023selectivecontext} showed that pruning low-information tokens preserves downstream accuracy; TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} apply selective trace extraction for automated debugging; and \citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit.
Our density decomposition complements these methods by quantifying \emph{why} compression helps (gradient dilution explains ${\leq}$24\% of the gap; the remainder reflects inference-time interference).

\subsection{Verdict Prediction and Fault Detection}

Verdict prediction is an instance of the longstanding test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle}.
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical program analysis with deep learning for defect detection.
In patch correctness prediction, representation learning of code changes has progressed from CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec} to LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} (84.4\%) and APPT \citep{appt2024} (79.7\%); \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness} evaluated change representations for predicting repair correctness.
FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated that structured fault signals (stack traces, mutation outcomes) improve localization; the equivalent-mutant problem \citep{papadakis2019mutation} poses an analogous classification challenge.
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra \citep{abreu2007accuracy,jones2002visualization,wong2014dstar}; recent LLM-based approaches such as AutoFL \citep{kang2024autofl} and AgentFL \citep{qin2024agentfl} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.
In agent-based repair, RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent}, Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless}, SWE-agent \citep{yang2024sweagent}, and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands} all incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows; in the SWE-bench ecosystem \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, these agents rely on test verdict signals to guide patch selection, yet which trace components carry that signal most efficiently remains unstudied.
LDB \citep{zhong2024ldb} applies segment-level trace verification for debugging, and SelfDebug \citep{chen2024selfdebug} and Reflexion \citep{shinn2023reflexion} iteratively refine code using execution outcomes.
None of these works isolate individual trace components or compare against rule-based baselines.

\subsection{Calibration and Training Dynamics}

Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration}, studies confidence--correctness alignment; \citet{spiess2025calibration} specifically addressed calibration for code models.
Our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 across four models suggests compact inputs improve calibration beyond accuracy gains alone.
Just-in-time defect prediction \citep{kamei2013large,hoang2019deepjit,pornprasit2021jitline} shares our fault detection motivation but operates on code change features rather than execution traces; our work complements this line by showing that execution-time fault signals can be classified with near-perfect accuracy when properly extracted.
Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} demonstrate that data quality and ordering improve convergence---consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable convergence within 50 steps while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation across all 444 training steps.
\citet{yang2024generalization} further showed that fine-tuned LLMs generalize better on concise inputs, providing a complementary perspective on why information density governs SFT effectiveness.

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces record a program's complete runtime behavior: every function call, variable assignment, and control flow decision.
Recent work has incorporated them into code language models for tasks from bug localization to program repair \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}, under the working assumption that richer runtime information yields better predictions.
\emph{We find the opposite.}
For verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), feeding a model the complete execution trace produces accuracies of 72--82\%, barely above a source-code-only baseline, while a single compact component of the same trace reaches ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models tested.
Verbose traces do not just fail to help; they actively impair learning.

Verdict prediction offers a clean testbed for isolating this effect.
As binary classification, it separates signal extraction from generation noise; as fault detection, the model need only detect failure, not simulate execution.
If the fault signal concentrates in a small trace subset, information density should matter more than quantity.
Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation tasks where this density hypothesis could not be cleanly tested.

We conduct the first systematic component ablation of trace representations, decomposing VOTA (exception events + assertion comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families \citep{qwen2025coder,roziere2024code,deepseek2024coder}, on 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}.
The results are unambiguous: exception events (a median of 150 tokens encoding error type, stack frame, and message) reach ${\geq}$99.33\% accuracy across all models and seeds, converging within 50 training steps.
Full traces oscillate between 82--89\% without stable convergence even under controlled gradient masking. This confirms that information density, not model capacity, is the binding constraint (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).

This finding is robust to several potential confounds.
Removing format markers preserves accuracy within 2pp, and on 8 boundary samples where exceptions appear in passing code, the fine-tuned model correctly classifies 6/8 vs.\ 0/8 for a regex baseline, which confirms the signal is semantic (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).
Gradient masking bounds the backward-pass contribution to ${\leq}$4pp (\S\ref{sec:density}), a tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}), and cross-dataset transfer to DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the component ranking (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).

Our contributions:

103	\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
104	\label{sec:vota_algorithm}
105	
106	Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.
107	
108	\begin{algorithm}[t]
109	\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
110	\label{alg:vota}
111	\small
112	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
113	\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
114	\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
115	\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
116	\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
117	\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
118	  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
119	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
120	\ENDFOR
121	\IF{no exception events found}
122	  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
123	\ENDIF
124	\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
125	\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
126	  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
127	  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
128	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
129	\ENDFOR
130	\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
131	\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
132	  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
133	    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
134	  \ENDIF
135	\ENDFOR
136	\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
137	\RETURN $V$
138	\end{algorithmic}
139	\end{algorithm}

253	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
254	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
255	
256	DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
257	Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, which confirms complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
258	The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
259	Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
260	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
261	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
262	Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).
263	
264	A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
265	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.
266	
267	Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
268	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).
269	
270	%% ============================================================
271	\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
272	\label{sec:irreducible}
273	
274	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
275	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
276	
277	\begin{itemize}
278	\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
279	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
280	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
281	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, which indicates a systematic rather than stochastic error.
282	\end{itemize}
283	
284	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
285	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
286	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
287	This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
288	
289	Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
290	However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
291	This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
292	The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.
293	
294	%% ============================================================
295	\section{Exception Type Accuracy Breakdown}
296	\label{sec:exception_type}
297	
298	Table~\ref{tab:exception_type} reports \texttt{exception\_only} accuracy stratified by exception type on Qwen-2.5-7B (seed=42, $N{=}1{,}190$).
299	All standard exception types (\texttt{TypeError}, \texttt{ValueError}, \texttt{IndexError}, etc.) achieve 100\% accuracy.

394	\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
395	Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).

400	\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
401	All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), which confirms that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.

405	\paragraph{Interpretation.}
406	These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
407	The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
408	The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
409	In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
410	
411	\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
412	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.

415	However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%). This indicates that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
416	The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
417	This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.
418	
419	The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).

617	\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
618	\label{sec:robustness_analysis}
619	
620	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
621	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
622	All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
623	VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
624	This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
625	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
626	The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.

\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, which confirms complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).

A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.

Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

\section{Irreducible Sample Analysis}
\label{sec:irreducible}

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, which indicates a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.

\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), which confirms that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.

However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%). This indicates that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
This is consistent with Python's execution model: exception tracebacks and assertion comparisons appear near the end of the trace but are preceded by the final function call frames, placing them typically 300--500 tokens from the terminus rather than at the absolute end.

The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

\section{Error Overlap Analysis}
\label{sec:error_overlap}

We analyze the overlap between error sets of different conditions to determine whether they fail on the same samples (Figure~\ref{fig:error_overlap}).

\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors (samples 901 and 905) have zero intersection with the error sets of all other conditions (Jaccard = 0.000 in all pairwise comparisons).
This orthogonality arises because \texttt{exception\_only} errors are caused by \texttt{GeneratorExit} false positives (pass samples misclassified as fail due to benign \texttt{BaseException} events), while errors from other conditions are predominantly fail samples misclassified as pass due to insufficient signal.

Among non-exception conditions, error sets exhibit hierarchical containment: \texttt{ae\_only} $\subset$ VOTA $\subset$ \texttt{loop\_only} $\subset$ \texttt{no\_trace}, with pairwise Jaccard indices increasing with signal overlap.
\texttt{loop\_only} and \texttt{full\_trace} share the highest overlap (Jaccard ${\sim}$0.65), reflecting their shared reliance on behavioral patterns rather than explicit fault indicators.

This analysis confirms that \texttt{exception\_only} operates on an independent signal dimension: its errors are representation ambiguities (iterator protocol artifacts) rather than information deficits, explaining why combining it with other signals cannot eliminate these specific errors.

\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness_analysis}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Execution Traces for Code LLMs}

Recent work has scaled trace-augmented training: TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} pre-trained on 2.6M execution-annotated samples, while \citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained models to predict execution outputs from traces.
\citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility to be task- and format-dependent but did not decompose individual trace components; relative to their work, we contribute a two-tier signal hierarchy, a phase transition in trace-length budgets, calibration analysis, and cross-architecture validation.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} leveraged trace chain-of-thought for execution reasoning, and \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, aligning with our density finding.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, extended to 19 languages by CRUXEval-X \citep{xu2025cruxevalx}, established execution reasoning benchmarks, though neither decomposes which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.
\citet{shi2023distracted} showed LLMs are easily distracted by irrelevant context, providing a complementary explanation for why verbose traces impair SFT learning.
In the prompt compression literature, LLMLingua \citep{jiang2023llmlingua} and Selective Context \citep{li2023selectivecontext} showed that pruning low-information tokens preserves downstream accuracy; TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} apply selective trace extraction for automated debugging; and \citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit.
Our density decomposition complements these methods by quantifying \emph{why} compression helps (gradient dilution explains ${\leq}$24\% of the gap; the remainder reflects inference-time interference).

\subsection{Verdict Prediction and Fault Detection}

Verdict prediction is an instance of the longstanding test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle}.
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical program analysis with deep learning for defect detection.
In patch correctness prediction, representation learning of code changes has progressed from CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec} to LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} (84.4\%) and APPT \citep{appt2024} (79.7\%); \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness} evaluated change representations for predicting repair correctness.
FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated that structured fault signals (stack traces, mutation outcomes) improve localization; the equivalent-mutant problem \citep{papadakis2019mutation} poses an analogous classification challenge.
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra \citep{abreu2007accuracy,jones2002visualization,wong2014dstar}; recent LLM-based approaches such as AutoFL \citep{kang2024autofl} and AgentFL \citep{qin2024agentfl} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.
In agent-based repair, RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent}, Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless}, SWE-agent \citep{yang2024sweagent}, and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands} all incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows; in the SWE-bench ecosystem \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, these agents rely on test verdict signals to guide patch selection, yet which trace components carry that signal most efficiently remains unstudied.
LDB \citep{zhong2024ldb} applies segment-level trace verification for debugging, and SelfDebug \citep{chen2024selfdebug} and Reflexion \citep{shinn2023reflexion} iteratively refine code using execution outcomes.
None of these works isolate individual trace components or compare against rule-based baselines.

\subsection{Calibration and Training Dynamics}

Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration}, studies confidence--correctness alignment; \citet{spiess2025calibration} specifically addressed calibration for code models.
Our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 across four models suggests compact inputs improve calibration beyond accuracy gains alone.
Just-in-time defect prediction \citep{kamei2013large,hoang2019deepjit,pornprasit2021jitline} shares our fault detection motivation but operates on code change features rather than execution traces; our work complements this line by showing that execution-time fault signals can be classified with near-perfect accuracy when properly extracted.
Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} demonstrate that data quality and ordering improve convergence---consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable convergence within 50 steps while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation across all 444 training steps.
\citet{yang2024generalization} further showed that fine-tuned LLMs generalize better on concise inputs, providing a complementary perspective on why information density governs SFT effectiveness.

10	\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
11	\label{sec:cross_model}
12	
13	Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares four models spanning three architecture families across a 1.5B--13B parameter range.
14	
15	\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}
16	Under \cond{exception\_only}, all four models converge to ${\geq}$99.33\% across all seeds, with a cross-model range of just 0.50pp---the tightest of any condition.
17	CodeLlama-13B reaches 100\% on one seed, confirming that the two persistent errors on Qwen (both \textit{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}) are convergence artifacts rather than hard data limitations.
18	
19	\paragraph{Scale invariance.}
20	Exception accuracy is independent of model scale: the smallest model (1.5B) matches the largest (13B) on the same representation (Figure~\ref{fig:cross_scale}).
21	In contrast, \cond{no\_trace} scales monotonically with capacity and exhibits the highest seed variance of any condition.
22	Exception events eliminate both the scale gap and the instability.
23	
24	\paragraph{VOTA robustness.}
25	Excluding one training failure caused by tokenizer-induced truncation (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}), VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models within a 0.80pp range.
26	The failure is itself informative: 91.7\% of that seed's training samples were truncated, while compact \cond{exception\_only} inputs (median 150 tokens) sidestep truncation entirely.
27	
28	\subsection{Component Ablation}
29	\label{sec:ablation}
30	
31	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} decomposes VOTA on Qwen-2.5-7B, revealing a two-tier hierarchy.
32	Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \cond{exception\_only} alone exceeds full VOTA, implying that combining additional components introduces noise rather than value.
33	Removing assertion points has no effect (\cond{VOTA\_no\_ae}), confirming exception dominance.
34	The Tier~1/2 boundary is sharp (Figure~\ref{fig:forest_plot}): the weakest Tier~1 condition exceeds the strongest Tier~2 by over 12pp with non-overlapping confidence intervals.
35	Tier~2 (\cond{loop\_only}) benefits are model-dependent: Qwen-7B gains +10.92pp over \cond{no\_trace} while CodeLlama gains only +0.93pp (n.s.), suggesting loop utilization reflects architectural capacity to exploit structured iteration patterns rather than a universal signal.
36	Within Tier~2, the larger Qwen-7B outgains Qwen-1.5B (+10.92 vs.\ +7.19pp, $p{<}.0001$), the only condition where scale provides a meaningful advantage.
37	
38	\paragraph{Baselines.}
39	The strongest regex heuristic (exception class name matching) trails SFT \cond{exception\_only} by 6.22pp ($p{<}.001$); the gap concentrates on boundary cases where SFT distinguishes caught from uncaught exceptions, correctly resolving 6/8 ambiguous samples vs.\ 0/8 for regex (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).

\section{Related Work}

\subsection{Execution Traces for Code LLMs}

Recent work has scaled trace-augmented training: TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} pre-trained on 2.6M execution-annotated samples, while \citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained models to predict execution outputs from traces.
\citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility to be task- and format-dependent but did not decompose individual trace components; relative to their work, we contribute a two-tier signal hierarchy, a phase transition in trace-length budgets, calibration analysis, and cross-architecture validation.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} leveraged trace chain-of-thought for execution reasoning, and \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, aligning with our density finding.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, extended to 19 languages by CRUXEval-X \citep{xu2025cruxevalx}, established execution reasoning benchmarks, though neither decomposes which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.
\citet{shi2023distracted} showed LLMs are easily distracted by irrelevant context, providing a complementary explanation for why verbose traces impair SFT learning.
In the prompt compression literature, LLMLingua \citep{jiang2023llmlingua} and Selective Context \citep{li2023selectivecontext} showed that pruning low-information tokens preserves downstream accuracy; TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} apply selective trace extraction for automated debugging; and \citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit.
Our density decomposition complements these methods by quantifying \emph{why} compression helps (gradient dilution explains ${\leq}$24\% of the gap; the remainder reflects inference-time interference).

\subsection{Verdict Prediction and Fault Detection}

Verdict prediction is an instance of the longstanding test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle}.
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical program analysis with deep learning for defect detection.
In patch correctness prediction, representation learning of code changes has progressed from CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec} to LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} (84.4\%) and APPT \citep{appt2024} (79.7\%); \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness} evaluated change representations for predicting repair correctness.
FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated that structured fault signals (stack traces, mutation outcomes) improve localization; the equivalent-mutant problem \citep{papadakis2019mutation} poses an analogous classification challenge.
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra \citep{abreu2007accuracy,jones2002visualization,wong2014dstar}; recent LLM-based approaches such as AutoFL \citep{kang2024autofl} and AgentFL \citep{qin2024agentfl} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.
In agent-based repair, RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent}, Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless}, SWE-agent \citep{yang2024sweagent}, and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands} all incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows; in the SWE-bench ecosystem \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, these agents rely on test verdict signals to guide patch selection, yet which trace components carry that signal most efficiently remains unstudied.
LDB \citep{zhong2024ldb} applies segment-level trace verification for debugging, and SelfDebug \citep{chen2024selfdebug} and Reflexion \citep{shinn2023reflexion} iteratively refine code using execution outcomes.
None of these works isolate individual trace components or compare against rule-based baselines.

Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration}, studies confidence--correctness alignment; \citet{spiess2025calibration} specifically addressed calibration for code models.
Our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 across four models suggests compact inputs improve calibration beyond accuracy gains alone.
Just-in-time defect prediction \citep{kamei2013large,hoang2019deepjit,pornprasit2021jitline} shares our fault detection motivation but operates on code change features rather than execution traces; our work complements this line by showing that execution-time fault signals can be classified with near-perfect accuracy when properly extracted.
Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} demonstrate that data quality and ordering improve convergence---consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable convergence within 50 steps while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation across all 444 training steps.
\citet{yang2024generalization} further showed that fine-tuned LLMs generalize better on concise inputs, providing a complementary perspective on why information density governs SFT effectiveness.
